title: Rate limiting and load shedding
description: Protect your API from traffic spikes and abusive clients. Learn rate-limiting algorithms, ASP.NET Core rate limiter middleware, and load-shedding patterns for high-traffic services.

data.text: Production APIs face sudden traffic spikes from flash sales, misbehaving clients, and bot traffic. Without guardrails, a spike can exhaust CPU, memory, or downstream database connections and take down every endpoint at once. Rate limiting and load shedding are complementary defenses: rate limiting prevents abuse over time, while load shedding makes hard cut decisions when the system is already under stress.

Choosing the right algorithm depends on your traffic pattern, memory budget, and fairness requirements. The four algorithms you will encounter in production are fixed window, sliding window, token bucket, and concurrency limiter.

items: Fixed window: allow N requests per minute. Simple, memory-light, but allows burst at window boundaries.
Sliding window: smooths out boundary bursts by tracking requests over a rolling interval. Better user experience but slightly higher memory cost.
Token bucket: refills tokens at a steady rate and allows short bursts up to the bucket size. Ideal for APIs that want to tolerate occasional spikes.
Concurrency limiter: caps the number of in-flight requests rather than counting over time. Perfect for protecting downstream services with limited connection pools.

data.text: ASP.NET Core 8+ includes built-in rate limiting middleware with token bucket, fixed window, and sliding window policies. It integrates with dependency injection and can partition limits by client ID, IP address, or any custom key.

data.title: Token bucket rate limiter

data.text: This configuration limits every authenticated client to 100 requests per minute with a queue depth of 10. Unauthenticated requests fall back to the IP address. When the limit is exceeded, the client receives 429 with a `Retry-After` header.

Rate limiting shapes traffic over time. Load shedding makes immediate decisions when the server is already overloaded. When CPU, memory, thread pool saturation, or downstream latency crosses a threshold, the API rejects new requests with 503 Service Unavailable instead of accepting them and degrading every caller.

items: Health-based shedding: check CPU, memory, or a downstream dependency before processing each request.
Queue-depth shedding: if the background work queue exceeds a depth, reject immediately.
Priority shedding: assign priorities to endpoints or clients and shed the lowest priority first.
Adaptive shedding: use recent error rate or p99 latency as the signal and adjust the allowed load dynamically.

data.title: Health-based load shedding middleware
Design caution
data.text: Load shedding is a last line of defense. If you rely on it often, your capacity planning is wrong. Use it for spikes, not normal traffic.

data.title: Key takeaways
items: Rate limiting controls traffic over time using token bucket, sliding window, or fixed window algorithms.
Use ASP.NET Core built-in rate limiter middleware with partitioned policies per client.
Return 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header so clients back off predictably.
Load shedding makes hard rejections when the system is already overloaded; treat it as a circuit breaker, not a replacement for capacity planning.
